title: Woodenization Example: Improving at Short Answer Questions + Teaching the Rubric he-rubric
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart walks through a concrete example of "Woodenization" -- his term for turning feedback into a deliberate, efficient teaching moment -- applied to scoring student Short Answer Questions (SAQs). After grading roughly 70 student responses using a single-point rubric, he compiled a short list of the most common writing problems and photographed how he'd marked them, then spent two to three minutes explicitly teaching students what those marks meant before returning the papers. He frames this brief teaching moment as serving two purposes at once: boosting his credibility with students (fast, expert-feeling turnaround) and helping students see the class content connecting to skills they already respect, like athletics. The piece is a compact case study in how quick, clear feedback routines can be converted into genuine instruction rather than just returned paperwork.
points: Woodenization in practice: converting a batch of graded rubrics into a targeted 2-3 minute mini-lesson on the most common errors, rather than silently handing papers back.
Stuart explicitly ties fast grading turnaround to teacher credibility, using an athletic-coaching analogy ("game feedback shortly after the game") that resonates with students' existing values.

His "Roots and Shoots List" method -- identifying the top three recurring problems before addressing any of them individually -- keeps the feedback session efficient and non-overwhelming for students.
The piece models how a purely logistical task (scoring rubrics) can be redesigned to double as instruction, assessment, and motivation in one short classroom moment.
quotes: Using our single-point rubrics (see pp. 184-185 in your copy of These 6 Things), I did my darnedest to have the ~70 student responses scored on the day they were submitted in class. I figured, "I'm going to be scoring these eventually, so why not dial myself in and get them scored quickly?
But if I were to just pass back the rubrics the next day without Woodenizing that part of the learning process, I'd leave a lot more learning potential on the table than I want to.
When I was done scoring, I made a list of my three biggest concerns with student writing quality (see "Roots and Shoots List" on pp. 181-183 of your copy of These 6 Things).

I've given these scores so quickly so you can improve your practice. Just like a good athletic coach is going to give you some game feedback shortly after the game concludes, so, too, I'll always try to do that with your writing.
This signals to the students that I know what I'm doing — a Credibility booster. It helps them attach the Value some of them have for athletics to the work we do in this class — a Value booster.
Woodenization is very simple, and we always want to make it as efficient as it can be. So much of this efficiency comes from the clarity we bring to the act.
